Why Small Models Still Matter

By Ada Example on September 14, 2026

Every few months a larger model arrives and the conversation shifts toward what it can do that the previous generation could not. That framing hides a quieter trend: compact models keep getting better at the narrow tasks that make up most real workloads, such as transcribing a meeting or reading a scanned invoice.

Running these models locally changes the economics. There is no per-request fee, no upload of sensitive audio to a third party, and latency is bounded by the machine on your desk rather than a queue in someone else's data center.

Quantization is the lever

Most of the gains come from quantization. Storing weights in four bits instead of sixteen cuts memory traffic by roughly a factor of four, and on unified-memory hardware memory bandwidth is usually the bottleneck for token generation.

  • Four-bit weights fit a 1.7B speech model in under a gigabyte.
  • Eight-bit weights recover most of the accuracy lost at four bits.
  • Mixed precision keeps embeddings and the output head at higher precision.

The fastest request is the one that never leaves the laptop.

What still needs work

Long-form audio remains tricky. Models trained on thirty-second clips drift on hour-long recordings, so practical pipelines segment the input, transcribe each piece, and stitch the results while guarding against repetition loops.

Document OCR has a different failure mode: tables and multi-column layouts. A model can read every word correctly and still produce an unusable result if it scrambles the reading order.
